rows.slideText: Uber. Next-Generation Car Service.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: We're Uber, and we're building the next generation of car service. Let me walk you through why getting a ride is ready for a change.
mustNotSay: [H] San Francisco or UberCab (not on this slide; production doesn't give the model a deck description)

rows.slideText: Problem. Most cabs in 2008 use aging & inefficient technology. Taxi-monopolies reduce the quality of service. No GPS coordination between client/driver.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: In 2008, most cabs ran on aging, inefficient technology. Taxi monopolies dragged down the quality of service, and there was no GPS coordination between the client and the driver.
mustMentionCritical: no GPS coordination between client and driver

rows.slideText: Solution. UberCab Concept: a fast & efficient on-demand car service. Automate dispatch to reduce wait-time. Latest consumer web & device technology. Optimized fleets and incentivized drivers.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Our solution is UberCab: a fast, efficient, on-demand car service. We automate dispatch to cut wait times, use the latest consumer web and device technology, and run an optimized fleet with incentivized drivers.

rows.slideText: How it Works. Client must be a member to use the service. Not hailed from the street but from your phone. Guaranteed Pick-up (unlike a yellow-cab). [image: phone mockups of the Uber app]
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Membership is required to use the service. You book rides from your phone, not by hailing on the street. And unlike a yellow cab, your pick-up is guaranteed.
mustMentionCritical: booked from your phone, not hailed on the street
mustNotSay: [H] Uber Eats / 'Order' or addresses read off the phone mockups

rows.slideText: Key Differentiators. 1-click hailing: "Pickup here in 5 mins". Members Only: Respectable clientele. Optimized fleet: Logistical LBS software. Fast Response Time: Easier than Calling. High Tech Solution: Geo-aware Auto-dispatch. Great Drivers: Rating System.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: What sets us apart: one-click hailing that's faster and easier than calling, a members-only service with respectable clientele, geo-aware auto-dispatch with an optimized fleet, and great drivers backed by a rating system.
mustNotSay: [N] response-time numbers other than the slide's 5-minute example

rows.slideText: Product. 1-Click request from Geo-aware devices. Book Trips, show Fleet status, trip history. Easy & Fast. [image: three app screenshots]
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: The product is built for speed. You request a ride with one click from any geo-aware device, and the same app lets you book trips, see fleet status, and check your trip history.
mustNotSay: [H] Uber Eats, music or other features seen in the mockups
[N] prices read off the mockups ($3.33 etc.)

rows.slideText: Use Cases. Trips to/from restaurants, bars & shows. Airport pickup/dropoff (pre-scheduled). Fast local transport where parking isn't easy. Working while commuting (wifi in cars).
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: We see four use cases: trips to and from restaurants, bars and shows; pre-scheduled airport pickups and drop-offs; fast local transport where parking isn't easy; and working while you commute, with wifi in the cars.
mustMentionCritical: fast local transport where parking isn't easy
mustNotSay: [O] bar trips described as pre-scheduled (pre-scheduled is the airport case)

rows.slideText: User Benefits. Cabs don't guarantee pickup, can take 45 mins. Cabs aren't as safe or clean as limos. Cars services.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Cabs don't guarantee a pickup, and one can take forty-five minutes to arrive. They also aren't as safe or clean as limos. We fix both.
mustMentionCritical: not as safe or clean as limos
mustNotSay: [O] 'pickup that never arrives' / 'often dirty' (stronger than slide)
[H] inventing meaning for the garbled third bullet 'Cars services'
slideLines: Cabs aren't as safe or clean

rows.slideText: Technology. Mobile phones + intelligent scheduling. Payment/utilization. Reputation tracking. Patent-pending system design.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Our technology pairs mobile phones with intelligent scheduling to handle payment and keep the fleet well utilized. We track reputation to keep quality high, and the system design is patent-pending.

rows.slideText: Market Size. [chart: unlabeled area chart, 2011-2016, y-axis 0-45] There are X target customers in the market. At our Y pricing, this is how large this company could become. Make sure to show the math on how you came to your conclusions. For more details: https://youtu.be/M_RMTC2YmXY. Source: Forrester / Gartner / your Uncle
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Here's how we think about market size: the number of target customers in our market, multiplied by our pricing, shows how large this company could become. We'll walk through the math behind that.
mustMentionCritical: target customers x pricing = how large the company could become
mustNotSay: [H] reading 'X' or 'Y' placeholders aloud as values
[N] any number or TAM from the chart (unlabeled axis)

rows.slideText: Looking Foward. Potential Outcomes. Best-Case Scenario: Becomes market leader, $1B+ in yearly revenue. Realistic Success Scenario: Gets 5% of the top 5 US Cities. Generates 20-30M+ per year profit. Worst-Case Scenario: Remains a 10 car, 100 client service in SF. Time-saver for San-Francisco based executives.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Three outcomes. Best case: market leader, over a billion dollars in yearly revenue. Realistic: five percent of the top five US cities, twenty to thirty million in yearly profit. Worst case: a ten-car, hundred-client service in San Francisco.
mustMentionCritical: best case: market leader, $1B+ yearly revenue
mustMentionOptional: worst case still a time-saver for SF executives

rows.slideText: Go-To Market plan. Referal: Invite only from an existing member. Virality: Become the ubiquitous "premium" cab service.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Our go-to-market runs on referral and virality. It's invite-only, so new members join through an existing member, and the goal is to become the ubiquitous premium cab service.
mustMentionCritical: referral: invite-only from an existing member
virality: become the ubiquitous premium cab service

rows.slideText: Traction. Progress to Date. October: California LLC + trademark filed. November: iPhone dev license applied for Nov. January: Bank Account + Paypal account. March: 5 advisors & 15 clients now.
rows.deckContext: Uber (UberCab) 2008 seed pitch: on-demand car service booked from your phone, launching in San Francisco.
rows.goldenScript: Our progress so far: a California LLC and trademark filing in October, an iPhone developer license application in November, and bank and PayPal accounts in January. Today we have five advisors and fifteen clients.
mustMentionCritical: iPhone dev license applied for (not granted)
mustMentionOptional: months: Oct LLC+trademark, Nov dev license, Jan bank+PayPal, Mar advisors/clients
mustNotSay: [O] dev license secured/granted (it was applied for)

rows.slideText: meesho. Turning Housewives into entrepreneurs. [photo: two women holding phones showing the Meesho Supply app]
rows.deckContext: Meesho 2016 Series A pitch: social-selling marketplace turning Indian housewives into resellers, starting on WhatsApp.
rows.goldenScript: Meesho is turning housewives into entrepreneurs, giving them an app to run their own reselling business straight from their phone.
mustMentionOptional: Meesho Supply app on a phone

rows.slideText: WHY SOCIAL SELLING? 200M+ Housewives in India Lots of Free Time Need Secondary Income SOCIAL SELLING Highly Social
rows.deckContext: Meesho 2016 Series A pitch: social-selling marketplace turning Indian housewives into resellers, starting on WhatsApp.
rows.goldenScript: There are over two hundred million housewives in India. They have lots of free time, they need a secondary income, and they're highly social. That makes social selling a natural fit.
slideLines: Lots of Free Time Need Secondary Income Highly Social

rows.slideText: SOCIAL SELLING 2.0 (Since Ancient Times) Local Boutiques/ Exhibitions (Since 2014) Multimedia Sharing became popular Dropshipping (Reselling) Kitty Parties 100X OPPORTUNITY • Direct Selling • (Amway Annual Revenue $1B) • 3 More Lucrative (Wider Collection & Reach) Low Barriers of Entry (No Investment) High Convenience (On Smartphone)
rows.deckContext: Meesho 2016 Series A pitch: social-selling marketplace turning Indian housewives into resellers, starting on WhatsApp.
rows.goldenScript: Social selling is ancient, from local boutiques and kitty parties to Amway's billion-dollar direct selling. Since 2014, multimedia sharing has turned it into reselling: a hundred-times opportunity, with wider reach, zero investment and just a smartphone.
mustMentionCritical: old model: boutiques/exhibitions, kitty parties, direct selling (Amway $1B)
more lucrative, no investment, on smartphone

rows.slideText: FAST GROWING MARKET! #Housewives Resellers ~0 2M (2014) (2017) 65% YoY 23M (2022 proj.) X Avg. Sales/ Reseller/ Month $330 (2017) = Total Addressable Market (TAM) $8B (2017) 4 50% YoY $50B (2022 proj.) SOURCE: ZINNOV CONSULTING
rows.deckContext: Meesho 2016 Series A pitch: social-selling marketplace turning Indian housewives into resellers, starting on WhatsApp.
rows.goldenScript: The market is growing fast. India had about two million housewife resellers in 2017, projected to reach twenty-three million by 2022. At three hundred thirty dollars a month each, that's an eight-billion-dollar market heading to fifty billion.

rows.slideText: RESELLING KOUDAI IN CHINA Weidian (Koudai) Launched in Jan 2014 Tools for Resellers on WeChat 50M $10B #Resellers on Weidian GMV Run Rate (Feb 2015) 70% $1.5B Shops from Tier 3 cities or below Valuation at last round Raised $ 350 mn from Tencent,Others 5
rows.deckContext: Meesho 2016 Series A pitch: social-selling marketplace turning Indian housewives into resellers, starting on WhatsApp.
rows.goldenScript: China's Weidian proves the model. Launched in 2014 with reseller tools on WeChat, it reached fifty million resellers and a ten-billion-dollar GMV run rate by February 2015, with seventy percent of shops in Tier 3 cities or smaller.
mustNotSay: [H] Alibaba or Amazon as the proof case
slideLines: Shops from Tier 3 cities or below Valuation at last round

rows.slideText: WHY CONSUMERS BUY FROM BUY? RESELLERS? WHY CONSUMERS Impulse Shopping Intent Shopping No need; Unique & Trendy Products Specific need; Need variety PERSONAL SHOPPER EXPERIENCE SOCIAL-PROOFED OUTBOUND INBOUND Social Selling CONSUMER OUTBOUND Ads 6
rows.deckContext: Meesho 2016 Series A pitch: social-selling marketplace turning Indian housewives into resellers, starting on WhatsApp.
rows.goldenScript: Consumers shop in two ways. With intent, they go looking on Amazon or Flipkart. On impulse, they respond to what reaches them, and a reseller's social-proofed recommendation works like a personal shopper, beating a Facebook ad.
mustMentionCritical: social selling = social-proofed outbound / personal shopper vs plain ads
mustMentionOptional: impulse: no need, unique & trendy products
mustNotSay: [O] social selling described as INBOUND (the slide shows it as social-proofed outbound
[H] discounts or lowest price as the reason
slideLines: No need; Unique & Trendy Products Specific need; Need variety

rows.slideText: HARD TO BE A RESELLER! It is very hard for a housewife to be a reseller because: Difficult Access to Supply No Price Visibility Low Trust b/w Resellers & Suppliers Personal connections or untrustworthy sourcing from FB; Larger suppliers inaccessible Cheated with high prices from Resellers No COD, No Returns, Many Fraud cases 7
rows.deckContext: Meesho 2016 Series A pitch: social-selling marketplace turning Indian housewives into resellers, starting on WhatsApp.
rows.goldenScript: It's very hard for a housewife to be a reseller. Supply is hard to access, prices aren't visible so resellers get overcharged, and trust is low, with no cash on delivery, no returns and frequent fraud.
mustMentionCritical: low trust between resellers and suppliers
mustMentionOptional: no COD, no returns, fraud cases
slideLines: It is very hard for a housewife to be a reseller because:
untrustworthy sourcing from FB; Cheated with high prices from Resellers No COD, No Returns, Many Fraud cases

notes.slideText: Flat visible text, one line (matches the Google Sheet).
notes.slideLines: The same text broken into lines the way Cloud Vision returns them. The runner's text mode feeds these, because structureSlideContent derives title/body from line breaks. Meesho: pdfplumber text layer (slides 1 and 19 replaced with the visible text; slide 5 title de-garbled). Uber: transcribed from the slide images, including chart axis labels and app-mockup text Vision would pick up.
notes.bannedTerms: Literal strings the rules grader matches (case-insensitive, whole word). Each comes from that row's must_not_say. The fuzzy must_not_say items are left to the LLM judge.
notes.split: About 20% of rows (stratified by difficulty, picked by a fixed hash) are 'holdout'. The runner saves only 'dev' rows by default. Tune prompts against dev; run --split holdout only to confirm a change before shipping, never while iterating.
